title: "Show us the straight path"
hook: the whole prayer is a request for directions, and the road has footprints on it
tomorrow: the call to prayer, and why it's beautiful even if you don't know the words

segments.voice: Yesterday: tawhid, You alone. Your line was simply one. Today, al-Fatiha finally asks for something. Day sixteen.

Think about the last time you were properly lost. Not a little turned around. Lost. The phone at two percent, the street signs in a language you can't read, every corner looking like the one before. What did you finally do? You stopped someone and asked: which way? It's a humbling question. And at the center of the prayer Muslims say most, after praise and mercy and trust, the one thing it asks for is directions.
screen: `PROPERLY LOST.` → `WHICH WAY?` → `THE PRAYER ASKS FOR DIRECTIONS.`

segments.voice: Verse six: “Show us the straight path.” In Arabic, ihdina s-sirata l-mustaqim. One word at a time. Ihdina: show us, guide us, from the root h-d-y, the same root as hidaya, guidance, and as hadiya, a gift. Guidance, in this language, is something handed to you. Sirat is a road, a wide, clear way. Mustaqim: straight, upright, not bending. Together, today's word: as-sirat al-mustaqim, the straight path. Notice the small word us. Even someone praying completely alone, at three in the morning, says show us. Then verse seven says whose path it is: “The path of those whom Thou hast favoured; Not (the path) of those who earn Thine anger nor of those who go astray.” Not an abstract rule, then, but a road with footprints on it. Another verse names those favored as the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous: the best of company. And two ways of missing it, which one common reading hears as knowing the way and walking off it, and never finding it at all. Muslims who pray ask for this road many times a day, for a lifetime. Why keep asking for a road you're already on? A simple answer: the path isn't found once. You ask to be shown it, and kept on it, at every corner. That's all seven verses, walked.
screen: `IHDINA — SHOW US, A GIFT.` · `SIRAT — A WIDE, CLEAR ROAD.` · `A ROAD WITH FOOTPRINTS ON IT.` · `ASKED AGAIN AT EVERY CORNER.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Bring to mind one place in your life where you honestly don't know which way to go: a decision, a relationship, a next step. Don't solve it. Stand at that corner for a moment and admit you don't know. Then picture one person who walked a hard road well, and the way they carried themselves. If you pray, you can carry the line in Arabic or English: show us the straight path.
As-sirat al-mustaqim. The straight path: a wide, clear road, asked for in every prayer, with footprints on it. Sixteenth word.
Your line: show us the way. Even praying alone, the prayer says us, not me. Day sixteen.

screen: `DAY 16 COUNTS. AL-FATIHA, ALL SEVEN VERSES.` → `TOMORROW: THE CALL TO PRAYER, AND WHY IT'S BEAUTIFUL.`

howItsDone: Muslims ask for the straight path in every unit of every prayer, and then recite verse seven to close al-Fatiha. Many also use the phrase in their own prayers, asking to be guided in a decision.

fork.setup: after five verses of praise and trust, al-Fatiha finally asks for something. what's the first thing it asks for?
options: to be shown the straight path.
fork.reveal: directions: show us the straight path. the request at the heart of the opening.

original.note: Arabic: the straight path. sirat, a wide road; mustaqim, straight, upright.

trapdoor: what you thought: a strict, narrow line you mustn't step off.
what it means: a wide, clear road, asked for as a gift, together, again and again, and walked by people who went before.
what a scholar hears: ihdina, from h-d-y, can mean both to show the way and to keep someone on it, which is how commentators answer why the guided keep asking; 4:69 names the favored.

notes: Moved: old day 11 → day 16, and it now carries verse seven too. The old day 12 (verse seven, word amin) was folded in here to make room in camp one for the two new week-one lessons (iman, Eid): its boot-prints idea, 4:69 and the 'two ways of missing it' reading are kept; the word amin and the angels' amin hadith are dropped from camp one (the Sunni/Shia difference on saying amin in prayer is a practice ruling better kept out of the first weeks). The close screen keeps 'al-Fatiha, all seven verses'.

Lightened: said once, Pickthall and Muslim no longer named in the spoken text, 'seventeen times a day' now 'many times a day', 'six verses down' cut, no homework in the carry, the practice keeps its sit without the bell line.

Many classical commentators, citing a hadith in Tirmidhi, identify 'those who earn anger' and 'those who go astray' with particular communities. The script deliberately gives only the general reading ('two ways of missing it') as 'one common reading'; a Keeper should confirm this is fair.
Qur'an 4:69 paraphrased (Pickthall's exact wording not certain), so quoted: null. Pickthall's 'favoured' is British spelling inside a quotation, which the guide allows.
Sirat as 'a wide, clear road': a common lexical gloss; confirm. Why the guided keep asking (to be shown and kept on the path): a standard tafsir answer, one of several; confirm.
